blocks.content: NULL Handling covered the broader behavior behind how SQL treats unknown values. SQL Aggregation Interview closes out the SQL Filtering and Aggregation module by combining everything covered across it, GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregate functions, and NULL handling, into the kind of real, practical questions that actually show up in technical interviews.

Aggregation questions are genuinely one of the most common SQL interview categories, precisely because they test whether you understand how these pieces combine, not just whether you can recite what each one does in isolation. This topic works through three genuinely representative worked questions.

1. How This Closes Out the Module
blocks.text: 1. How This Closes Out the Module

blocks.content: Looking back across the module makes the connection clear. GROUP BY collapsed rows into groups. HAVING filtered those grouped results. Aggregate functions actually computed the values GROUP BY and HAVING rely on. COUNT versus COUNT star covered a genuinely subtle, common distinction. NULL handling covered the broader behavior behind that distinction and others like it.

This closing topic combines all five into the kind of question a real interview actually asks, since interview questions rarely test one isolated concept, they genuinely test whether you can combine several pieces correctly under real pressure.

blocks.content: 2. The Genuinely Common Interview Question Shape
blocks.text: 2. The Genuinely Common Interview Question Shape

blocks.content: A genuinely common shape for these questions asks you to find the department, group, or entity meeting some real, specific threshold, more than a certain count, above a certain average, below a certain total. This genuinely requires GROUP BY and HAVING working together, not just one or the other alone.

These questions also often involve a specific, deliberate choice between aggregate functions, count versus sum versus average, and the right choice depends entirely on genuinely understanding what the actual question is asking for.

3. Worked Question One

Find every department with an average salary above 75000. This genuinely requires grouping by department, computing the average salary per group, and then filtering those grouped results by that computed average.

SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary)>75000;
blocks.code:
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary)>75000;

codes.sql:
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary)>75000;

blocks.content: GROUP BY department creates one group per department. AVG salary computes the actual average within each group. HAVING then filters, keeping only departments where that computed average genuinely exceeds 75000, discarding the rest from the final result.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438413956-948434944.png
4. Worked Question Two
Find customers who placed more than three orders. This genuinely requires grouping by customer, counting orders per customer, and filtering to only the customers whose count genuinely exceeds three.

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*)>3;
blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*)>3;

codes.sql:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*)>3;

blocks.content: GROUP BY customer_id creates one group per customer. COUNT star counts every order row within each group, genuinely counting orders regardless of any NULL values elsewhere in the row. HAVING then keeps only customers whose order count genuinely exceeds three.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438413956-117947129.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Writing WHERE COUNT star greater than 3 instead of HAVING, one of the single most common errors in exactly this kind of interview question, tracing directly back to the real SQL execution order covered earlier in this course.
5. Worked Question Three

Find the average order value across all orders, treating any missing discount as zero rather than letting it silently vanish from the calculation. This genuinely requires combining AVG with COALESCE to handle NULL discounts correctly.

SELECT AVG(amount-COALESCE(discount, 0)) AS avg_net_value
FROM orders;
blocks.code:
SELECT AVG(amount-COALESCE(discount, 0)) AS avg_net_value
FROM orders;

codes.sql:
SELECT AVG(amount-COALESCE(discount, 0)) AS avg_net_value
FROM orders;

blocks.content: COALESCE discount, 0 substitutes zero specifically wherever discount is genuinely NULL, ensuring every single order genuinely contributes to the average, rather than having orders with a NULL discount subtly skew the calculation in an unintended way.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438413957-494756051.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A genuinely strong interview answer explains not just the working query, but why each specific piece is actually needed, why HAVING instead of WHERE, why COALESCE instead of assuming NULL behaves like zero automatically.
6. Genuinely Common Traps

A few real traps show up constantly in this specific category of interview question. Using WHERE instead of HAVING for the actual threshold condition, which genuinely fails since WHERE runs before the aggregate value even exists. Forgetting that NULL values silently vanish from SUM and AVG, rather than being treated as zero, which can genuinely skew a calculation without any obvious error.
And confusing COUNT star with COUNT of a specific column, silently undercounting whenever that specific column happens to contain NULL values in some rows.

items: Aggregation interview questions genuinely test combining GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregate functions together, not each in isolation.
The common question shape asks for groups meeting a real threshold, genuinely requiring GROUP BY and HAVING together.
HAVING, not WHERE, is the correct clause for filtering on any computed aggregate value.
COALESCE is a genuinely practical tool for treating a NULL value as a specific default within a calculation.
COUNT star and COUNT of a specific column can genuinely produce different results whenever that column contains NULL.
A genuinely strong answer explains the reasoning behind each clause choice, not just a working query with no explanation.
